text:
Write \(\operatorname{Gr}(k,10)\) for the Grassmannian of \(k\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb C^{10}\). Let \(\Pi\subset\operatorname{Gr}(3,10)\) be the Zariski closure of the row spaces of matrices \(A=(a_1\ \cdots\ a_{10})\) satisfying
\[
a_{2i}=\lambda_i a_{2i-1},\qquad \lambda_i\in\mathbb C^\times\quad(1\le i\le5),
\]
where every three vectors among \(a_1,a_3,a_5,a_7,a_9\in\mathbb C^3\) are linearly independent. Define
\[
X=\{V\in\operatorname{Gr}(4,10):V\subset C^\perp\text{ for some }C\in\Pi\},
\]
where orthogonality uses the bilinear form \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{10}x_i y_i\), without complex conjugation. Let \(R=\mathbb C[\operatorname{Gr}(4,10)]\) denote the homogeneous coordinate ring of the affine Plücker cone, with \(\Delta_I\) the determinant in the increasingly ordered columns indexed by \(I\) of a generic \(4\times10\) matrix. You may assume that \(X\) is an irreducible hypersurface and that its homogeneous ideal \(I(X)\subset R\) is principal.

The following conventions specify the basis and the normalization of the generator to be computed. A tableau \(T=I_1|\cdots|I_N\) is a rectangular array with four rows, entries in \(\{1,\ldots,10\}\), strictly increasing columns and weakly increasing rows. Its content \(\gamma_s\) is the number of occurrences of \(s\). The classical standard monomials \(P_T=\Delta_{I_1}\cdots\Delta_{I_N}\) form a basis of \(R\). Order tableaux with the same number of columns lexicographically by the word obtained by reading each row from left to right, starting with the top row. Let \(F\) be the homogeneous generator of \(I(X)\), normalized so that the coefficient of the lexicographically smallest tableau occurring in its standard-monomial expansion is \(1\).

To define the classical dual canonical elements \(b(T)\) precisely, take an indeterminate \(q^{1/2}\) and the algebra over \(\mathbb C[q^{\pm1/2}]\) generated by \(u_{as}\), \(1\le a\le4\), \(1\le s\le10\), with relations
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{as}u_{at}&=q\,u_{at}u_{as} &&(s<t),\\
u_{as}u_{bs}&=q\,u_{bs}u_{as} &&(a<b),\\
u_{at}u_{bs}&=u_{bs}u_{at} &&(a<b,\ s<t),\\
u_{as}u_{bt}-u_{bt}u_{as}&=(q-q^{-1})u_{at}u_{bs} &&(a<b,\ s<t).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(I=\{i_1<i_2<i_3<i_4\}\), set
\[
\Delta_I^q=\sum_{\sigma\in S_4}(-q)^{\ell(\sigma)}u_{1,i_{\sigma(1)}}u_{2,i_{\sigma(2)}}u_{3,i_{\sigma(3)}}u_{4,i_{\sigma(4)}},
\]
where \(\ell(\sigma)\) counts inversions, and let \(R_q\) be the subalgebra generated by these minors. The bar operation fixes \(\mathbb C\) and every \(u_{as}\), sends \(q^{1/2}\) to \(q^{-1/2}\), and satisfies \(\overline{fg}=\overline g\,\overline f\). Put
\[
P_T^q=\Delta_{I_1}^q\cdots\Delta_{I_N}^q,\qquad
\widetilde P_T=q^{-\beta(T)/2}P_T^q,\qquad
\beta(T)=4\binom N2-\sum_{s=1}^{10}\binom{\gamma_s}{2}.
\]
For tableaux of the same shape and content, define
\[
c_{h,r}(T)=\sum_{a=1}^h\#\{\text{entries at most }r\text{ in row }a\},
\]
and write \(S\prec T\) when \(c_{h,r}(S)\le c_{h,r}(T)\) for all \(1\le h\le4\), \(1\le r\le10\), with at least one strict inequality. Let \(b_q(T)\) be the unique element satisfying
\[
\overline{b_q(T)}=b_q(T),\qquad
b_q(T)=\widetilde P_T+\sum_{S\prec T}c_{T,S}(q)\widetilde P_S,\qquad
c_{T,S}(q)\in q^{-1}\mathbb Z[q^{-1}],
\]
and set \(b(T)=b_q(T)|_{q^{1/2}=1}\).

Determine the complete finite set of pairs \((T,a_T)\) with \(a_T\ne0\) in the expansion
\[
F=\sum_T a_T\,b(T).
\]
Specify each tableau by its ordered list of columns and give every coefficient exactly.

The answer was proved recently, so it is not an open problem: your task is to find it and prove it, completely, and to write Python that really computes or checks every step that can be checked. Printing what you believe is not evidence. Arriving at an answer that settles less than the question asks (a partial or conditional answer, "not known") is not acceptable, and neither is conceding: when an approach fails, try another.

Proving it means showing that the answer is right in every case the question covers, and that no other answer is.

Stop only when your proof is complete. When you stop, write in that response what you proved, and what is left.
